lessons.title: Capital Flows, Crude Oil and the Dollar Index: The Rupee's Big Three

children.text: Look at the rupee's situation in September 2026. FPIs have pulled ₹2.37 lakh crore out of Indian shares so far this year. Brent crude has been trading above $100 a barrel. And the US dollar index is holding near 99 as markets bet on a Fed rate hike. The rupee is sitting near 95.5 per dollar. None of these three forces is Indian, and India's current account deficit is small. Yet together they explain most of what the rupee does week to week. This lesson gives you a working model of the rupee's big three, so you can read a rupee headline and know which force is behind it.

body.text: In the short run, the rupee is mostly a price set by three things India does not control: foreign portfolio money, the price of crude oil and the strength of the US dollar worldwide. When all three turn against the rupee together, RBI can slow the fall but cannot stop it.

children.text: Force 1: Capital Flows

markDefs.definition: An environment where global investors cut exposure to riskier assets, such as emerging-market shares and currencies, and move money into safer assets like US Treasuries and the dollar.

children.text: You already know FPIs are the fastest money in the rupee market. What moves them is mostly global. Rising US bond yields make safe dollar assets more attractive. Expensive Indian valuations push funds towards cheaper markets. A
risk-off
episode, a war, a banking scare or a carry trade unwind makes funds sell emerging markets across the board. In each case, foreign investors sell rupee assets and buy dollars, and the rupee weakens.

body.context: Already more than the ₹1.66 lakh crore withdrawn in the whole of 2025, per NSDL data.

children.text: The FPI outflow alone was more than twice the current account deficit. That is the pattern to remember: in most quarters, the swing in portfolio flows is bigger than the swing in trade. A year earlier, in Q1 FY26, FPIs had brought in a net $1.6 billion. The difference between those two quarters, an $11.2 billion swing, is worth more to the rupee than any change in India's trade balance over the same period.
Force 2: Crude Oil

children.text: India imports close to nine of every ten barrels it refines, and pays for them in dollars. When crude rises, Indian Oil, BPCL, HPCL and private refiners need more dollars for the same volume. That is direct, daily dollar demand in the interbank market. But oil hits the rupee through more than one door, which is why it is such a powerful force.

body.title: The five ways a crude spike reaches the rupee

children.text: Dollar demand.
Oil companies buy more dollars to pay for each cargo.
Wider deficit.
The current account deficit grows, so India needs more capital inflows to fund it.
Higher inflation.
Fuel, freight and fertiliser costs push up Indian inflation, eroding the rupee's real return.
Fiscal strain.
If the government cuts fuel taxes or raises subsidies to shield consumers, its borrowing can rise.
FPI nerves.
Foreign investors see all of the above and trim Indian exposure, adding capital outflows on top of the trade effect.

body.title: The cost of $10 a barrel
body.prompt: India has recently imported close to 5 million barrels of crude oil a day. Using 5.0 million barrels a day as a round figure, if the average crude price is $10 a barrel higher for a full year, how much larger is India's annual crude import bill, in $ billion? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: 5.0 million barrels × $10 × 365 days = $18,250 million, or $18.25 billion a year. That is more than four times the entire current account deficit of Q1 FY27. Every one of those extra dollars has to be bought in the forex market.

children.text: Force 3: The US Dollar Index

markDefs.definition: The US Dollar Index, or DXY. It measures the dollar's value against a weighted basket of six developed-market currencies, starting from a base of 100 in March 1973.

children.text: Sometimes the rupee falls not because anything happened to the rupee, but because the dollar rose against everything. The best single gauge of that is the
US Dollar Index

, or DXY. It does not include the rupee, but when the DXY climbs, emerging-market currencies, including the rupee, usually weaken too. In mid-September 2026 the DXY was around 99, while markets were pricing in a possible Fed rate hike.

body.caption: What the Dollar Index is made of

body.title: The euro drives the index
body.prompt: Suppose the euro rises 2% against the dollar and every other currency in the DXY basket is unchanged. Using the weights, by roughly what percentage does the DXY fall? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: Approximate change = euro weight × euro move = 57.6% × 2% = 1.15%. A stronger euro means a weaker dollar, so the DXY falls about 1.15%. This is why the DXY is sometimes called a euro index in disguise: to understand the DXY, first check EUR/USD.

body.text: The big three rarely move independently. A crude spike pushes up US inflation, which raises the odds of a Fed hike, which lifts US yields and the DXY, which pulls FPI money out of India. One oil shock can turn on all three forces at once. That clustering is why the rupee's worst stretches, like 2013, 2022 and 2026, tend to arrive as perfect storms rather than single shocks.

body.title: Best week for the rupee
body.question: Which combination is most likely to strengthen the rupee over a week?
options: Brent up 8%, DXY up 1.5%, FPIs selling
Brent down 6%, DXY down 1%, FPIs buying Indian bonds
Brent down 6%, DXY up 2%, FPIs selling heavily
Brent flat, DXY flat, gold imports surging
body.explanation: Cheaper crude cuts dollar demand from oil importers, a weaker dollar globally lifts emerging-market currencies, and FPI bond buying brings dollars in. All three forces point the same way. The other options have at least one or two forces working against the rupee.

body.text: Do not trade the rupee on one headline. A crude spike can be offset by a falling DXY. FPI selling can be absorbed by RBI intervention. And markets react to surprises versus expectations, not to the news itself. The scorecard helps you understand moves after they happen and judge the balance of risks. It is not a signal system.

body.title: A week in the rupee market
body.scenario: Monday: Brent crude jumps from $102 to $110 after supply disruptions in the Gulf. Tuesday: US inflation data comes in hotter than expected, and futures markets raise the odds of a Fed hike. The DXY climbs from 99 to 100.5. Wednesday: NSDL shows FPIs sold ₹6,000 crore of Indian shares over two days. Thursday: a large Indian conglomerate announces a $3 billion FDI deal with a Japanese partner, with money arriving over the next two years. Friday: USD/INR, which started the week at 95.50, touches 96.40 and then stalls as state-run banks sell dollars.
body.prompt: Walk through the week using the big three. Which forces were active each day, how did they connect, what did the FDI announcement change, and what explains Friday's stall?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Monday, crude: an 8% jump in Brent raises dollar demand from oil importers and widens the expected current account deficit. Rupee negative.
2. Tuesday, dollar index: hot US inflation raises Fed hike bets, lifts US yields and pushes the DXY up 1.5%. Emerging-market currencies weaken broadly. Rupee negative. Note the link: higher oil feeds higher US inflation too.
3. Wednesday, capital flows: FPIs sell, partly reacting to Monday and Tuesday. Rupee negative. All three forces now point the same way.
4. Thursday, FDI: the deal is positive for the capital account, but the money arrives over two years, so it barely affects this week's dollar demand. Stable funding helps the medium-term picture, not the immediate move.
5. Friday: the rupee falls 90 paise in a week, then stalls as state-run banks sell dollars, the classic sign of RBI intervention to curb volatility. RBI slows the move but has not reversed any of the three forces, so pressure is likely to persist until crude, the DXY or FPI flows turn.

body.title: Your weekly big-three rupee tracker
steps: Note the week's change in Brent crude and whether it is above or below $100.
Note the week's change in the DXY and the US 10-year Treasury yield.
Check cumulative FPI equity and debt flows for the week on NSDL.
Check whether any Fed or RBI meeting, US inflation print or US jobs report is due.
Mark each force as rupee positive, negative or neutral, and compare with how USD/INR actually moved.
Where the rupee moved less than the forces suggest, look for signs of RBI intervention in news reports.

body.textWithBlank: The currency with the largest weight in the US Dollar Index, at 57.6%, is the ___.
body.explanation: The euro makes up more than half of the DXY basket, so EUR/USD moves drive most of the index's day-to-day changes.

cards.definition: When global investors dump riskier assets like emerging-market shares and currencies for safer ones like the dollar.
Foreign portfolio investors selling Indian shares or bonds and converting rupees to dollars. The fastest force on the rupee.
The share of India's crude needs met by imports, about 89% in FY26.
The US Dollar Index, measuring the dollar against six developed-market currencies, dominated by the euro.
When capital outflows, rising crude and a strong dollar hit the rupee at the same time, as in 2013, 2022 and 2026.
Every $10 rise in crude is estimated to widen India's current account deficit by about 0.4% to 0.5% of GDP.

points: Capital flows, crude oil and the US Dollar Index drive most of the rupee's short-term moves, and none of them is controlled by India.
FPI flows usually swing more than trade flows. In Q1 FY27, the $9.6 billion FPI outflow was more than twice the current account deficit.
India imports about 89% of its crude. Oil spikes hit the rupee through dollar demand, the deficit, inflation, fiscal strain and FPI nerves.
The DXY measures the dollar against six developed currencies, with the euro at 57.6%. A rising DXY usually drags the rupee down.
The big three tend to move together: oil shocks raise US inflation and Fed hike odds, which lift the dollar and push FPIs out.
Use a simple scorecard to understand rupee moves, and look for RBI intervention when the rupee moves less than the forces suggest.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or trading advice. Market levels, flow data and rules of thumb are approximate and as of the dates stated, drawn from NSDL, RBI, PPAC and market reports. The crude volume used in the exercise is an illustrative round figure.
